questions.prompt: Why is InheritedFromUniqueProcessId alone not sufficient to prove a live parent-child relationship existed at the time of acquisition?
options: It's always inaccurate and should never be trusted
It's a stored value recorded once at process creation, not a live pointer -- it says nothing about whether that parent PID still exists or was ever reused
It only exists on Windows Server, not workstations
It's encrypted and cannot be read from memory
questions.explanation: InheritedFromUniqueProcessId is a stored PID value from process creation time. Since PIDs get reused constantly, a stored parent PID that no longer maps to any running process is expected behavior, not automatically suspicious on its own.

questions.prompt: How does DKOM (Direct Kernel Object Manipulation) hide a process while it keeps running?
options: It terminates the process and creates a hidden replacement
It patches the Flink/Blink pointers in ActiveProcessLinks so list-walking tools skip over the process entirely, without affecting the separate scheduling mechanism that keeps it executing
It encrypts the process's memory space
It changes the process's PID to a random value
questions.explanation: Unlinking from ActiveProcessLinks only affects enumeration -- tools that walk that list simply never encounter the process. The Windows scheduler uses a separate mechanism, so the process keeps running normally, just invisible to standard enumeration.

questions.prompt: Why does psscan successfully find a DKOM-hidden process that pslist misses?
options: psscan asks the process directly whether it's hidden
psscan scans the raw memory image for the EPROCESS pool tag signature rather than walking the ActiveProcessLinks list, finding the structure regardless of whether anything currently links to it
psscan only works after a system reboot
psscan and pslist actually use the identical method
questions.explanation: A DKOM-hidden process is unlinked from the list pslist reads, but its EPROCESS structure -- with the same pool tag as any other -- is still sitting in memory, which is exactly what psscan's pool-tag scan is designed to find.

questions.prompt: What does the PEB (Process Environment Block) pointer in an EPROCESS structure lead to?
options: User-mode-accessible memory holding the process's own self-reported view of its loaded modules and command line
A list of all other processes running on the system
questions.explanation: The PEB is what dlllist and cmdline actually read from -- it's the process's own self-report of its modules and command line, which is why cross-referencing it against other sources (like ldrmodules does) can reveal discrepancies.
